title-group.article-title: Water Rules and Land Rules: Adaptive Spatial Production and Post-Weir Crisis at Lake Tempe, Indonesia

abstract.p: Wetland ecosystems across Southeast Asia are undergoing profound socio-ecological transformations driven by hydraulic infrastructure interventions; however, scholarly attention to the spatial-relational dimensions of these transformations remains limited. This study examines how the space of Lake Tempe has been produced and reconfigured amid long-term sedimentation and hydraulic intervention, drawing on Henri Lefebvre’s theory of the production of space as its analytical framework. Employing a qualitative approach with a single case study strategy, the research draws on in-depth interviews with seven informants representing diverse actor categories—including fishers, farmers, government officials, customary leaders, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs)—complemented by field observation and documentary analysis. The findings yield three central insights. First, prior to the ecological crisis, Lake Tempe was organized through a dichotomy of water-based and land-based customary rules, encompassing five adaptive spatial typologies that were integrated through a spiritual-cosmological dimension exemplified by the Maccera’ Tappareng ritual—a ritual in which offerings are ceremonially released into the lake. Second, informants associated the Movable Weir, operating since 2013, with the curtailment of the dry-season recession on which this differentiation depended; Tanah Koti and Balete are reported to be no longer practiced, and local ecological knowledge is weakening. These changes unfolded alongside other drivers and intensified inequalities of access that predated the weir. Third, this crisis has catalyzed a spatial reconfiguration marked by the emergence of new actors such as the pa’tassi (operators of passenger transport boats), who operate according to a tourism-driven economic logic. Theoretically, this study extends Lefebvre’s framework to a non-Western, rural-aquatic context by incorporating a spiritual-cosmological dimension into the concept of representational space, while also showing how state-led infrastructure can act as a compounding force in the erosion of the commons. For sustainable wetland governance, the findings point to the need to include customary institutions and local ecological knowledge in decisions about the weir’s operation, so as to support livelihood continuity and equitable access to common resources.

sec.title: 1. Introduction
sec.p: Wetlands and floodplain ecosystems across Southeast Asia are currently undergoing socio-ecological transformations of unprecedented magnitude, driven by the convergence of hydraulic infrastructure development, climate change, and the commodification of natural resources (Folke et al., 2021; Pokhrel & Tiwari, 2022; Soukhaphon et al., 2021). From the Mekong basin to the rivers of Sulawesi, state interventions in hydrological regimes through dams and irrigation schemes have fundamentally reordered the seasonal rhythms that have long sustained the livelihoods of millions who depend on inland fisheries and wetland agriculture (Dang et al., 2022; Fiorella et al., 2023). These transformations extend well beyond ecological change; they disrupt customary institutions, local ecological knowledge systems, and social structures that have evolved over centuries (Müller-Mahn et al., 2021).

As an archipelagic nation encompassing hundreds of significant lakes and wetland ecosystems, Indonesia stands at the forefront of these transformations. Lake Tempe, one of the largest floodplain lakes in South Sulawesi, has experienced significant ecological transformation over the past decades, with sediment accumulation reaching 20–40 cm annually, which has severely reduced its storage capacity (Cahyono et al., 2024). In response to this degradation, large-scale infrastructural interventions—including a phased dredging program, the construction of artificial islands from dredged material, and the establishment of flood embankments and a Movable Weir at the downstream outlet—have been implemented under the coordination of the Ministry of Public Works (Cahyono et al., 2024). However, these interventions, alongside continuous land degradation in the catchment area, have produced a multidimensional crisis that reverberates across thousands of fisher and farmer households, as well as the indigenous Bugis communities surrounding the lake, prompting community-led adaptive responses rooted in local wisdom (Harifuddin et al., 2025).

Four bodies of work frame this study. First, research on wetland commons in Southeast Asia has examined how access to floodplain fisheries is allocated and contested. In Cambodia’s Tonle Sap, for instance, a century-old system of auctioned fishing lots was abolished in 2012 in favor of community fisheries, with mixed social and ecological outcomes (Chan et al., 2020; KC et al., 2020). Second, scholarship on the politics of hydraulic infrastructure has shown that dams and weirs reorder not only flows of water but also relations of authority over territory and livelihoods (Boelens et al., 2016; Dang et al., 2022; Soukhaphon et al., 2021). Third, studies of local ecological knowledge emphasize the role of customary institutions in adaptive resource governance (Berkes, 2012); at Lake Tempe, recent work has documented customary prohibitions, local fisheries institutions, and community responses to degradation (Harifuddin et al., 2025; Jumiati et al., 2024). Fourth, Lefebvre’s theory of the production of space has increasingly been applied beyond Western cities—to rural spaces (Halfacree, 2007), to environmental questions (Foster et al., 2020), and to villages in China (Wang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025).

What these strands have not yet brought together is an account of how space is produced in a seasonally pulsing lake whose governance rests simultaneously on customary institutions, a religious cosmology, and state hydraulic infrastructure. Research on Lake Tempe has concentrated mainly on hydrology, flood risk, and fisheries (Cahyono et al., 2024), and inland lake fisheries in Indonesia have received less attention than marine small-scale fisheries (Stacey et al., 2021). The relations among actors, rules, and cosmology through which the lake’s space is produced—and how these relations change when the seasonal recession is curtailed—therefore remain largely unexamined. Applications of Lefebvre, for their part, have to our knowledge seldom addressed spaces whose very identity alternates with the seasons. This gap matters for sustainability: the continuity of wetland livelihoods, equitable access to common resources, and the survival of local ecological knowledge all depend on how such spatial relations are reorganized when hydraulic infrastructure intervenes.

Accordingly, this research analyzes the patterns of spatial utilization at Lake Tempe amid long-term sedimentation and hydraulic intervention, employing Henri Lefebvre’s theory of the production of space as its interpretive lens. The central research question is: How has the space of Lake Tempe been produced and reconfigured through the interplay of actor practices, institutional arrangements, and local cosmology—against a background of long-term sedimentation and, more specifically, since the Movable Weir began operating—and what does this reconfiguration imply for livelihood continuity, equitable access to common resources, and the survival of local ecological knowledge? To address this question, the study adopts a qualitative approach with a single case study strategy, drawing on in-depth interviews, field observations, and documentary analysis.

This study makes three contributions to understanding sustainability challenges in floodplain wetlands. First, it refines the application of Lefebvre’s production of space to a seasonally pulsing, rural-aquatic setting, showing how space at Lake Tempe was produced cyclically through the alternation of water rules and land rules, and how representational space was structured by a Bugis-Islamic cosmology with concrete institutional effects. Second, drawing on informants’ accounts and regulatory documents, it traces how relations among the three dimensions of Lefebvre’s triad became increasingly hierarchical after the Movable Weir began operating. Third, it argues that hydraulic infrastructure acted as a compounding force rather than a sole cause, intensifying enclosure dynamics already underway through auction-based capitalization and the privatization of Tanah Koti. Together, these contributions suggest that livelihood continuity, equitable access to common resources, and the survival of local ecological knowledge depend not only on hydrological targets but also on who takes part in defining them.

sec.title: 2.1. Research site profile
sec.p: This study was conducted in the Lake Tempe region, a floodplain lake situated in the central part of South Sulawesi Province, Indonesia, geographically positioned between 4°00'–4°15' South latitude and 119°51'–120°06' East longitude. The lake spans the administrative territories of three regencies—Wajo, Soppeng, and Sidenreng Rappang—with the majority of its water body falling under the jurisdiction of Wajo Regency. To provide clearer geographic orientation, Figure 1 illustrates the position of Lake Tempe within the broader context of the Indonesian archipelago and the island of Sulawesi.

caption.title: Research location map—Lake Tempe, South Sulawesi, Indonesia

sec.p: From a hydrological standpoint, the lake receives inflows from two principal watersheds—the Bila River Basin to the north and the Walanae River Basin to the south—while discharging outflows through the Cenranae River Basin, which empties into the Gulf of Bone. This hydrological system generates pronounced seasonal water-level dynamics characteristic of floodplain lakes in the region, where surface areas can expand and contract dramatically between dry and rainy seasons, fundamentally shaping the patterns of resource use by surrounding communities (Cahyono et al., 2024; Kimijima et al., 2020).

The present condition of Lake Tempe results from several overlapping processes that operate on different time scales. The first is long-term sedimentation, driven largely by erosion in the catchment, which has progressively reduced the lake’s storage capacity (Cahyono et al., 2024). The second comprises state infrastructural responses to this degradation. The Movable Weir on the Cenranae River, completed in 2013, was designed to maintain the lake at an elevation of +5.00 m throughout the year, sustaining a dry-season inundated area of about 132.9 km² (Rifai et al., 2016). A revitalization program followed, in which sediment was dredged from the lake and the dredged material used to construct artificial islands (Juliastuti et al., 2025), and Lake Tempe was later designated a national priority lake (Government of Indonesia, 2021). The third consists of hydrometeorological factors: the lake has long been subject to recurrent floods fed by runoff from upstream tributaries, notably the Walanae and Bila Rivers, and drains into the Gulf of Bone through the Cenranae River (Darma et al., 2025), and informants additionally linked recent inundation to erratic rainfall.

Two features of the chronology in Table 1 shape our analysis. First, the Movable Weir was explicitly designed to prevent the lake from receding in the dry season—an objective documented in technical sources rather than inferred from informants’ accounts alone (Rifai et al., 2016). In its first year of operation, however, this target was not reached: in the 2014 dry season the lake remained at +3.50 to +4.50 m, partly because the main gates were frequently opened at the request of residents around the lake and downstream (Rifai et al., 2016). Second, informants dated the onset of prolonged, non-receding inundation to between 2019 and 2021, several years after the weir began operating. These accounts differ in emphasis and should be read together. Technical monitoring shows that the lake still receded in the 2014 dry season, to levels close to its pre-weir dry-season range (Rifai et al., 2016), whereas Informant 2 described the water as not having receded since 2014, and Informant 4 dated prolonged inundation to 2019, which followed major floods in 2018 and 2019 (Cahyono et al., 2024). We do not read these accounts as contradictory. Informant 2 dated the decline of his Palawang earnings (income from the demarcated fishing ground) to 2014, but his statement, made in 2025, describes that decline through the conditions prevailing at the time of the interview and thus compresses a longer process. Informant 4’s account, by contrast, refers to the point at which farmland ceased to emerge at all. Taken together, the sources suggest that the dry-season recession weakened gradually rather than ceasing in 2013, with prolonged inundation becoming established from about 2019. This temporal pattern suggests that the weir interacted with other drivers rather than producing all subsequent changes on its own. This study does not attempt to apportion causal weight among these drivers, which would require hydrological modelling beyond its scope; rather, it examines how actors experienced, interpreted, and adapted to these changes. Accordingly, we use the term “post-weir” to denote the period after 2013, not to imply that the weir alone produced every change observed within it.

sec.p: The selection of Lake Tempe as the research site rests on three substantive considerations. First, Lake Tempe constitutes a strategic aquatic ecosystem that has sustained the livelihoods of thousands of Bugis fisher and farmer households for centuries, thereby offering an empirically rich context for examining the dynamics of spatial production within an agrarian-aquatic society. Second, the lake is currently facing a significant socio-ecological crisis precipitated by sedimentation and the operation of the Movable Weir since 2013, rendering it a living laboratory for understanding how infrastructural interventions reshape customary institutions and local practices. Third, the enduring presence of the Maccera’ Tappareng tradition—a ritual in which offerings are ceremonially released into the lake—and indigenous ecological knowledge systems such as Pananrang, a traditional Bugis system for forecasting seasonal cycles, affords a degree of ethnographic richness that is comparatively rare among other aquatic ecosystems in Indonesia. The fieldwork was concentrated in several urban villages (kelurahan) and villages (desa) bordering the lake, with particular attention to Kelurahan Laelo and Kelurahan Salomenraleng, both of which directly adjoin the principal utilization zones of Lake Tempe. The selection of these micro-locations was guided by the diversity of actors engaged in lake-based activities—including fishers, farmers, pa’palawang (those who work the palawang, a demarcated fishing area with regulated boundaries and dimensions), pa’tassi (operators of passenger transport boats), customary leaders, village administrators, and local non-governmental organizations (NGOs)—as well as by the researchers’ practical access to key informants.

sec.title: 2.2. Research design
sec.p: This study employs a qualitative approach with a single-case study strategy, as developed by Yin (2017) and further elaborated by Johnson (1996) in the form of the intrinsic case study. The qualitative approach was selected because the research seeks to understand the meanings, experiences, and social relations embedded in the spatial utilization practices of Lake Tempe—a dimension that cannot be adequately captured through quantitative approaches oriented toward statistical generalization (Creswell & Poth, 2016). The single-case study strategy was adopted because Lake Tempe possesses distinctive and idiosyncratic characteristics—namely, the confluence of a seasonal water-level system, the Maccera’ Tappareng tradition, and the post-weir crisis—that render it a case of intrinsic value warranting in-depth examination, rather than a representative sample of a broader population of lakes (Johnson, 1996).

The theoretical framework guiding the research design is the theory of the production of space proposed by Lefebvre (1991), particularly the conceptual triad distinguishing among spatial practice, representations of space, and representational space. This framework was chosen because it enables a holistic analysis of spatial dynamics—conceived not merely as a physical entity, but also as a social construct and a lived space mediated through symbols and cosmology. The application of Lefebvrian theory to this non-Western, rural-aquatic context further aligns with recent developments in the literature that call for extending Lefebvre’s framework beyond the European urban settings in which it was originally formulated (Biagi, 2020; Schmid, 2022).

The research was conducted over a six-month period, with the field data collection phase concentrated in August 2025. This timing was determined by substantive considerations: traditionally, August marks the peak of the dry season—the musim timur (East Monsoon) in the Bugis Pananrang—which should correspond to the period of maximum water recession and the activation of land-based customary rules. Conducting observations during this period enabled the researchers to assess directly the extent to which traditional seasonal rhythms remain operative, while also coinciding with the peak of tourism activity carried out by the pa’tassi. The months preceding and following the data collection phase were devoted to instrument preparation, secondary document review, transcription, coding, and report writing. The study was guided by an interpretive epistemological stance, which positions knowledge as constructed through the meanings that actors ascribe to their practices (Denzin & Lincoln, 2011). This stance was operationalized analytically through reflexive thematic analysis, as elaborated in the subsequent section.

sec.title: 2.3. Data collection
sec.p: Data collection was conducted through three complementary techniques: field observation, in-depth interviews, and documentary analysis. The combination of these methods served as a form of methodological triangulation aimed at strengthening the credibility of the findings (Patton, 2014). Field observation was carried out directly at several spatial utilization sites—Palawang, Bungka Toddo, Rawa, and the activity zones of the pa’tassi—with the aim of understanding everyday spatial practices, including the ways in which fishers operate their fishing gear, the social dynamics emerging within collective activities, and the physical-ecological conditions of the spaces in use. Field notes were recorded continuously throughout the observation period to capture contextual details that often remain unarticulated in interviews (Joffe, 1996).

In-depth interviews were conducted with seven informants selected through purposive sampling (Patton, 2014), whose profiles are summarized in Table 2. Potential informants were identified through three channels: the kelurahan administration (local urban village government), the Macoa Tappareng (the traditional customary leader of the lake), and the research team’s own networks. The last channel reflects the fact that a member of the research team had previously worked as a community empowerment facilitator in the area, which provided prior familiarity with actors possessing deep knowledge of the lake’s problems. From this pool, seven informants were selected according to three criteria: (1) direct involvement in lake-based spatial practices as fishers, farmers, pa’palawang, or pa’tassi; (2) a regulatory or customary position, whether in local government or in customary institutions such as the Macoa Tappareng; and (3) engagement in community advocacy through NGOs. Each informant was chosen because they occupied a distinct position within the spatial relations of the lake and were locally recognized as knowledgeable about its governance and change. The aim of this composition was not representativeness within each actor category but diversity across positions (polyvocality), so that each dimension of Lefebvre’s triad could be examined from the vantage points of differently positioned actors.

We acknowledge that this prior engagement shaped the research in two ways. It facilitated access and trust, enabling candid discussion of sensitive matters such as criticism of government policy and knowledge regarded as sacred. At the same time, it oriented recruitment toward recognized and articulate local figures already known to the team. Less visible actors—for instance, small-scale fishers without community standing, or women engaged in lake-based livelihoods—are therefore underrepresented, and informants’ familiarity with a team member may also have influenced how they framed their accounts. We sought to mitigate these effects through triangulation with documents and field observation and by attending closely to divergences among accounts.

Consistent with reflexive thematic analysis, which treats data saturation as an ill-fitting criterion (Braun & Clarke, 2021), we assessed the adequacy of the material using the concept of information power (Malterud et al., 2016). Information power was supported by the specificity of the informants’ experience—each had long-standing, direct involvement in the space or institution concerned—by the use of an established theoretical framework as a sensitizing device, by the depth of the interviews (60–120 minutes, conducted in informants’ everyday settings), and by triangulation with regulatory documents and field observation. We nonetheless acknowledge that several actor categories are represented by a single informant. Variation within categories—for instance, among fishers using different gear or operating at different scales, or among farmers with different tenure arrangements—could therefore not be captured. We accordingly present informants’ statements as positioned accounts rather than as the views of their categories as a whole, and we indicate throughout whether a claim rests on one account, several accounts, or documentary evidence.

The interviews were conducted using a semi-structured interview guide that outlined the principal research themes while affording the researchers latitude to follow the informants’ narrative flow and to explore themes that emerged organically (Patton, 2014). Each interview lasted between 60 and 120 minutes and was held in settings where informants felt at ease—predominantly in their own homes, along the lakeshore, or at the sites of their daily activities—so as to foster an egalitarian and non-intimidating conversational atmosphere. With the informants’ consent, the interviews were audio-recorded and subsequently transcribed verbatim for analysis. In addition to observation and interviews, documentary analysis was undertaken by examining a range of secondary sources, including Wajo Regency Regional Regulation No. 4 of 2012 on Fishery Resource Management (Wajo Regency Government, 2012) and local media coverage of Lake Tempe management policy (Fajar, 2016).

sec.title: 2.4. Data analysis
sec.p: Data analysis was conducted using a thematic analysis approach, specifically the reflexive thematic analysis developed by (Braun & Clarke, 2019; Braun & Clarke, 2022). This approach was selected because it enables the systematic identification and interpretation of patterns of meaning emerging from the field data, while simultaneously accommodating researcher reflexivity throughout the interpretive process. The analysis proceeded through six interrelated phases: (1) familiarization with the data through repeated readings of interview transcripts and field notes; (2) generation of initial codes that flagged units of meaning within the data; (3) searching for themes by clustering related codes; (4) reviewing themes against the data; (5) defining and analytically naming the themes; and (6) producing the report by integrating the themes into a coherent narrative (Braun & Clarke, 2022).

The analysis proceeded in two movements. In the first, the data were coded openly and inductively. Two members of the research team coded the interview transcripts and field notes manually, generating initial codes that stayed close to informants’ own language and practices—for example, “borrowing capital to enter the auction” or “the water no longer recedes”. The resulting codes were clustered into candidate themes, which were then reviewed jointly by all five members of the research team against the full data set and refined before being defined and named. Consistent with reflexive thematic analysis, this collective review served to question and deepen interpretation rather than to establish inter-coder agreement (Braun & Clarke, 2019). Only in the second movement were the developed themes read against Lefebvre’s triad, which functioned as a sensitizing concept (Bowen, 2006) rather than as a predetermined coding frame.

Table 3 illustrates this progression for each of the five final themes. The reading was not one of simple allocation. Some themes corresponded to more than one dimension of the triad, and one—the seasonally alternating character of space—exceeded the triad’s distinction among perceived, conceived, and lived space. Rather than forcing this theme into a single dimension, we retained it and drew on Lefebvre (2013) rhythmanalysis to interpret it (Section 4). The five final themes structure the presentation of the Results: the first three in Section 3.1, the fourth in Section 3.2, and the fifth in Section 3.3.

sec.title: 2.5. Research ethics
sec.p: This study was conducted with a full commitment to the principles of qualitative research ethics as articulated in contemporary methodological scholarship (Iphofen & Tolich, 2018; Tracy, 2019). Prior to each interview, every informant was provided with an explanation of the research objectives, the right to decline answering particular questions, the right to withdraw at any time, and the manner in which their data would be used and protected. Consent was obtained orally and recorded at the outset of each interview, a practice better suited to the Indonesian cultural context than written consent forms, which can introduce a formal distance between researcher and informant (Liamputtong, 2010).

With respect to confidentiality, the identities of all informants in this study were protected through the use of numerical codes (Informant 1 through Informant 7) in the presentation of the data. The decision to anonymize all informants was grounded in the recognition that not all informants were comfortable with the disclosure of their identities, particularly where their narratives contained criticism of government policy or revealed traditional knowledge regarded as sacred. Beyond anonymization through coding, the researchers also exercised careful contextualization by omitting details that might enable external parties to identify informants—such as highly specific residential locations or readily recognizable formal positions. In line with this principle, Table 2 reports age ranges and general role categories rather than exact ages, specific positions, or villages, and these details have also been omitted from the presentation of the findings. The one exception is Informant 6, whose position as Macoa Tappareng is central to the analysis of customary governance; he agreed during the recorded consent procedure to the disclosure of this position. In this study, ethics is understood not merely as a procedural formality but as an integral dimension of the human relationship between researcher and informants, one that positions informants as partners in the production of knowledge rather than as mere sources of data (Tracy, 2019).

sec.title: 3.1. The adaptive spatial typology of lake tempe: water rules and land rules
sec.p: The watershed system described in Section 2.1 (Figure 2) generates the seasonal water-level fluctuations around which the communities surrounding the lake have long organized their space.

caption.title: Map of the Lake Tempe river basin system

sec.div: From this hydrological system emerges a conceptual dichotomy that lies at the very core of the entire spatial utilization system of Lake Tempe: the water rules (ade’ allopi-loping) and the land rules (ade’ tana). Informant 1, a government official with extensive experience in lake governance, articulated this dichotomy in clear terms:
sec.p: “During the rainy season, when the entire lake area is inundated, the water rules apply—that is, the rules governing fishing. During the dry season, the land rules take effect—the rules concerning cultivation” (Informant 1, interview, 2025).

The statement indicates that the space of Lake Tempe was understood not as fixed but as changing its identity with the hydrological cycle: water, and the domain of fishers, in the wet months; land, and the domain of farmers, in the dry months. In Lefebvre (1991) terms, space is produced through social practice; at Lake Tempe, this production was cyclical—a rhythm we return to in Section 4.

This emic understanding of water rules and land rules gives rise to five types of traditional utilization spaces, each possessing its own distinctive physical character, access mechanisms, and associated actors: Rawa, Palawang, Tanah Koti, Balete, and Bungka Toddo. These five spaces are not merely spatial categories but socio-ecological institutions that regulate the relationship between the community and the lake’s resources.

Rawa is the most open of the five spaces: seasonal pools linked to the surrounding rivers, allocated communally through annual application to the local government and bounded by permanent stakes (Table 4).

sec.p: Palawang is more structured: a semicircular fishing enclosure of bamboo belat, whose dimensions we confirmed through field observation, allocated through an annual auction held by the regency government (Table 4). Although the auction is formally open to any fisher, Informant 2’s account shows that participation depends on resources beyond fishing skill. Informant 2, a pa’palawang, described the complexity of this mechanism on the basis of his own experience:

“At the time, I borrowed 20 million rupiah from my father to participate in the auction. I completed the bidding requirements and submitted them to the committee, and I secured a Palawang site in Sabbangparu. I partnered with someone who owned the equipment to operate it, since I did not yet possess the necessary gear, such as the belle. I still manage Palawang today; in fact, I currently operate two Palawang sites” (Informant 2, interview, 2025).

The resources his account points to are financial capital (the 20 million rupiah of initial funding) and social capital (partnership with an equipment owner). His management of two sites at once suggests that the auction can enable a concentration of control, although our data do not allow us to assess how widespread this is.

A similar transformation was reported in Tanah Koti, an agricultural space historically allocated to residents through a lottery system (koti in the Bugis language means “to be drawn by lot”). In the past, the lottery mechanism ensured the rotation and equitable distribution of land among residents on an annual basis. However, Informant 3, a senior fisher, explained the fundamental shift that has taken place:
“In the past, Tanah Koti ownership involved no private possession (ongko); now private ownership has emerged” (Informant 3, interview, 2025).

The term ongko in Bugis tradition refers to a temporary usufruct right vested in the community rather than the individual. The shift from ongko to private ownership represents a paradigmatic transformation from a system of communal rights toward a system of private rights—a shift we interpret as a form of enclosure in the sense discussed in scholarship on land and exclusion in Southeast Asia (Hall et al., 2011). According to Informant 3 and the documentary sources summarized in Table 4, this transformation has occurred through formal channels such as land ownership certificates and land tax assessment documents (Surat Pemberitahuan Pajak Terutang, SPPT), as well as through informal channels such as hereditary inheritance from the descendants of the Datu/Raja and former village officials.

Balete integrates agriculture and fisheries within a single unit: an embanked paddy that serves as rice land in the dry season and as a fish trap as the water recedes (Table 4). It is therefore a locus of coordination between farmers and fishers, whose interests must be reconciled within the same space.

Bungka Toddo operates according to yet another logic, using clumps of aquatic vegetation held in bamboo frames as a trapping medium (Table 4). Vegetation often regarded as a “pest” from a technocratic perspective is thus used as ecological infrastructure for fish spawning.

The utilization system of these five spaces cannot be understood in isolation from the spiritual-cultural dimension that accompanies it. These spaces are not merely sites of economic production but also arenas of interaction with supernatural forces. Informant 6, a Macoa Tappareng (customary lake elder), explained the cosmology underlying the activities conducted in these spaces:

“In every village, before the beginning and at the end of the fishing season within a single annual cycle, a customary ritual is performed—known as Maccera’ Tappareng or maddupa’ wai (welcoming the rising water)—to honor the ruler of the waters, the guardian of the lake (ya makuasae)” (Informant 6, interview, 2025).

The Maccera’ Tappareng ritual—literally meaning “to feed the lake” or “to purify the lake”—is led by Informant 6 in his capacity as Macoa Tappareng, assisted by the Pabbijagae (generally women). This ritual marks the opening and closing of the fishing season while also serving as a medium of symbolic negotiation between the human community and the ya makuasae. Alongside this collective ritual, a system of taboos (pamali) governs the individual conduct of fishers, encompassing prohibitions against fishing from Thursday evening until after Friday prayers, against carrying two fishing implements at once, against singing in the boat, against quarreling with fellow fishers, against using foul language (moni’sala), and against bringing women along during fishing activities. In addition, there exist sacred sites (makerre’), marked by thickets and large trees (aju colo’ and kawerrang), that must be kept free from fishing activity.

According to Informant 6, violations of these customary rules were historically subject to a sanction known as idosa, with penalties consisting of eight liters of glutinous rice (aruwa gantang), eight combs of bananas, and eight chicken eggs—the recurring number eight representing cosmological perfection in Bugis tradition. Beyond material fines, social sanctions were enacted through the public announcement of the offender’s name at the mosque and the confiscation of the offender’s boat until the fine was paid. Although, in his account, these sanctions have since been converted into monetary fines agreed with the Macoa Tappareng, he described their normative structure as still in force.

The complexity of this spatial typology and its entanglement with the spiritual dimension demonstrates that before the weir, Lake Tempe was organized as an adaptive and locally grounded socio-ecological system in which productive practices, social regulation, and cosmology were closely interwoven—though, as the cases of Palawang and Tanah Koti show, not one free of internal inequality. Table 4 summarizes the character of these five spaces along with their current utilization status, providing the foundation for understanding the disruption to be discussed in the following subsection.

sec.title: 3.2. The disruption of adaptive space: the movable weir and the loss of the dry-season recession
sec.p: The adaptive spatial typology outlined in the preceding subsection describes a socio-ecological system that had taken shape and operated over the course of centuries, grounded ontologically in the dynamics of seasonal water-level fluctuation. Since 2013, however, this system has confronted a fundamental structural disruption through the operation of the Lake Tempe Movable Weir—a large-scale hydraulic infrastructure designed to regulate the lake’s water elevation at +5.00 m above sea level. From a technocratic standpoint, the weir was intended to maintain the lake’s water level, control flooding, and secure downstream water needs; it was justified partly on the grounds that low dry-season water levels hindered fishing and farming around the lake (Rifai et al., 2016). Yet its central operating principle—keeping the lake from receding in the dry season—curtailed the very recession on which several of the adaptive spaces described above depended.
Informant 1, the government official who earlier explained the dichotomy between water rules and land rules, described the structural impact of the Movable Weir in unequivocal terms:

“At present, the water-level fluctuation pattern has all but ceased to occur. Several types and sites of management within Lake Tempe no longer rely on that pattern—Tanah Koti (lottery-allocated land) and Balete land, for instance, no longer exist. Those that remain, such as Bungka Toddo, Palawang, and Rawa, along with the Tanah Patok Belanda (Dutch-stake land), still persist, but no longer function optimally” (Informant 1, interview, 2025).

Informant 1’s statement points to two consequences. First, in this account, spaces premised on seasonal change lose their operational logic when the dry-season recession fails to occur: Tanah Koti emerges only when the water recedes, and Balete depends on the transition between seasons. Second, the spaces that persist were reported to yield less, since they too depend on water-level fluctuation. In Informant 1’s account, then, two of the five adaptive spaces are no longer practiced and the remaining three operate below their former capacity. As the chronology in Table 1 shows, these changes unfolded over several years and alongside other drivers, which is why we read the weir as a compounding rather than a sole cause.

Informant 1 reported that “the majority of fishers opposed the 2013 operational policy of the Movable Weir, which maintained the water at an elevation of +5.00 m”—an assessment we could not verify independently, although Informants 4 and 7 likewise described the persistently high water level as harmful to their livelihoods, and Informant 7 relayed residents’ view of a different ideal water height at the weir (see below). Informant 1 grounded this opposition in what was described as the community’s local knowledge: “according to the community’s local knowledge, fish can only reproduce effectively when they follow the water-level fluctuation pattern” (Informant 1, interview, 2025). We interpret this disagreement as more than a technical dispute over water elevation: it sets knowledge grounded in hydraulic engineering against knowledge built from long experience of the lake’s seasonal rhythms.

The empirical impact of this disruption manifests differently across each group of actors, producing what may be termed a polyphony of crisis—the diversity of experiences and actor voices responding to the same situation from divergent socio-economic positions. Table 5 summarizes this polyphony, which is analyzed in greater detail in the paragraphs that follow.

sec.p: Informant 2 described the losses on his auction investment:

“Since 2014, when the weir came into operation, Palawang earnings have steadily declined because the water level has never receded since. As things stand now, three years have passed since the auction and we have yet to see any returns; the belat gear cannot be installed because the water remains permanently high. The Palawang is utterly dependent on water-level fluctuation—the longer the recession period, the better the yield” (Informant 2, interview, 2025).

His situation reveals a paradox: an investment made through a state-organized auction depends on the very recession that the weir’s operation has curtailed. In our reading, two arms of the state thus operate according to contradictory logics, and the burden falls on actors such as Informant 2.

At the level of farming households, the impact has been even more severe. Informant 4, a farmer who is also a community religious figure, reported that the prolonged flooding has entirely severed access to agricultural activity:

“Farming activities can no longer be conducted at present because, to this day, Lake Tempe’s water has never receded. Lake Tempe has been in flood since 2019, compounded by erratic weather and by overflow rainfall arriving from Sidrap and Soppeng Regencies” (Informant 4, interview, 2025).

In Informant 4’s account, the prolonged inundation was compounded by erratic weather and by hujan kiriman—overflow rainfall arriving from Sidenreng Rappang and Soppeng. His account thus points to the interaction of infrastructural and hydrometeorological factors outlined in Section 2.1, which is why we do not attribute these changes to the weir alone.
Informants also reported changes in the lake’s fish community. Informant 3, a senior fisher, described this shift:

“Around the 1980s and 1990s, fish yields in Lake Tempe were abundant and were even exported beyond Sulawesi. The lake’s fish species included tilapia (Ikan Nila), snakehead (Ikan Gabus), and Ikan bungo. Today, however, these species have become increasingly scarce, while Ikan Patin (pangasius catfish) and Ikan Sapu-sapu (suckermouth catfish) have appeared in their place” (Informant 3, interview, 2025).

Informant 4 linked the scarcity of ikan bungo (Glossogobius giuris) to a decline in fishing activity: “since ikan bungo has disappeared from Lake Tempe—a fish that fishers once routinely caught for consumption and sale—fishers now rarely venture out onto the lake to fish” (Informant 4, interview, 2025). These accounts describe a perceived shift in species composition, which informants associated with the altered condition of the lake. Part of this picture is independently documented: the Amazon sailfin catfish (Pterygoplichthys pardalis)—the ikan sapu-sapu mentioned by Informant 3—has been recorded as an invasive species with an increasing population in Lake Tempe (Tamsil et al., 2024). Our data cannot establish how far these changes are attributable to the weir rather than to the other drivers outlined in Section 2.1; they indicate that, for fishers, the post-weir period is experienced as one of declining and changing catches.

A more subtle yet equally consequential dimension of this crisis is the weakening of local ecological knowledge—particularly the Pananrang system, the traditional Bugis knowledge of reading natural signs to determine the seasons. Informant 4 explained that this system has become difficult to apply:

“Lake Tempe today no longer follows the two-season pattern (musim barat and musim timur), because conditions have become difficult to read and increasingly unpredictable. In the past, the community could foresee the arrival of the western and eastern monsoons through what is called Pananrang (the signs for reading the seasons). The rainy season was marked by November, and the planting season by June” (Informant 4, interview, 2025).

Informant 4’s account suggests that Pananrang is losing its predictive reliability. If the seasonal regularity on which it rests does not return, the transmission of this knowledge to younger generations may also be at risk—a possibility our data can raise but not assess. This resonates with the argument proposed by Berkes (2012) that traditional ecological knowledge is sustained through ongoing practice and may erode when the conditions that support that practice are disrupted.
Informant 7, representing the policy oversight NGO, raised the issue of the artificial islands:

“The cause of sedimentation lies in the nine islands that were constructed… Lake Tempe’s water has now not receded for four years, causing widespread hardship; many homes have been damaged… according to local residents, the ideal water height at the weir is 2 meters” (Informant 7, interview, 2025).

Informant 7 attributed the lake’s sedimentation to the artificial islands built from dredged material; our data cannot test this claim. Informant 7 also conveyed residents’ view that the ideal water height at the weir is 2 m. This figure is expressed in local terms and may not correspond directly to the +5.00 m elevation above sea level used in the weir’s official operation; the two should therefore not be read as points on a single scale. The gap between them nonetheless marks a contestation over the configuration of Lake Tempe’s space. Although hydrological assessment would be needed to evaluate any operating level (Section 4), the disagreement is also one of values: over what kind of space ought to be produced, and by and for whom.

Taken together, informants’ accounts describe the post-weir period as one in which a lake organized around seasonal alternation has come to function, in their experience, more like a reservoir held at a persistently high level. The changes they report—the disappearance of Tanah Koti and Balete, declining yields in Palawang and Bungka Toddo, damage to homes, fish eggs failing to hatch, the spread of an invasive species, and the weakening of Pananrang—have multiple drivers. Yet the water that no longer recedes runs through almost every account as the change that made the others harder to absorb.

This crisis, however—as the following subsection will demonstrate—is not solely a story of loss. The disruption has also opened space for the emergence of new actors operating according to distinct economic and spatial logics—some of whom reinforce dependence on prolonged inundation rather than resist it.

sec.title: 3.3. The emergence of new actors and the reconfiguration of space: pa’tassi and tourism
sec.p: The disruption outlined in the preceding subsection has given rise to a paradoxical phenomenon at Lake Tempe: amid the destruction of traditional adaptive spaces, new spaces have emerged with a distinct socio-spatial logic—spaces no longer governed by the dichotomy of water rules and land rules, but rather by the logic of the market and commodification. The emergence of these new actors, particularly the pa’tassi as water transport operators and NGOs as advocacy actors, demonstrates that ecological crisis does not merely produce loss; it also gives rise to complex socio-spatial reconfigurations. Within the theoretical framework of Lefebvre (1991), this phenomenon can be understood as a form of new spatial production unfolding through the dialectic between disruption and adaptation—a process in which old spaces are erased while, simultaneously, new spaces are born to fill the vacuum left in their wake.

The most prominent actor in this reconfiguration is the pa’tassi, the local designation for boat-based water transport operators on Lake Tempe. Informant 5, a pa’tassi active in the lake area, situated the emergence of this occupation within the context of the post-weir hydrological crisis:
“Pa’tassi activities have only been carried out over the past three years, because Lake Tempe’s water still has not receded—the level remains permanently high” (Informant 5, interview, 2025).

This statement carries important implications. The pa’tassi is not a long-standing occupation that has subsequently undergone transformation; rather, it is an actor born of the crisis itself, a profession that emerged in response to the prolonged inundation. Herein lies its fundamental paradox: the very condition that has harmed fishers and farmers—the water that never recedes—constitutes the economic precondition for the pa’tassi’s existence. The pa’tassi thus occupy a structurally ambiguous position: their occupation emerged in response to the crisis, yet its material continuity depends on the continuation of the very conditions that have harmed fishers and farmers.
Organizationally, the pa’tassi are structured in a relatively formal manner. Informant 5 described the institutional architecture that has taken shape:

“The pa’tassi of Lake Tempe are divided into two groups, with thirty members in each group. The boats used by the pa’tassi around Lake Tempe are katinting-type vessels equipped with 65-PK engines, with a maximum capacity of seven passengers… The operations of the pa’tassi at Lake Tempe are governed by a queueing system coordinated by a designated overseer (coordinator)” (Informant 5, interview, 2025; field observation, 2025).

The total of approximately sixty pa’tassi organized into two groups, each with its own coordinator, points to the existence of a relatively institutionalized form of informal organization. The queueing system administered by a coordinator represents what Ostrom (1990) terms a self-governing institution—a collective-arrangement institution that emerges from below to manage access to a common-pool resource (in this case, access to passengers). Yet unlike Lake Tempe’s traditional governing institutions (the Macoa Tappareng, the auction system, and the Tanah Koti lottery), the pa’tassi institution is rooted neither in Bugis cosmology nor in local government regulation, but rather in the rationality of the service market.
A more incisive dimension of the pa’tassi phenomenon is reflected in the differentiated tariff structure they apply. Informant 5 described the prevailing pricing arrangement:

“For fares, passengers pay 7,000 rupiah per person—this applies particularly to local residents and domestic passengers. The situation is different for tourists, who pay 700,000 rupiah (as a charter fee) for a single destination trip to the central area of Lake Tempe (Sallo Tengah). These tourists come from the Netherlands and the United Kingdom, and from several neighboring countries” (Informant 5, interview, 2025).

The two prices are not directly comparable: 7,000 rupiah is a per-person fare for local passengers, whereas 700,000 rupiah is the charter price of a boat carrying up to seven passengers to Sallo Tengah—about 100,000 rupiah per passenger even at full capacity. Together, however, they suggest what may tentatively be characterized as a dual economy of space—a configuration in which the same space (the waters of Lake Tempe) generates radically different economic values depending on who consumes it. For local residents, water transport is a basic necessity born of prolonged inundation that has cut off land-based access routes. For foreign tourists, the same waters constitute an object of aesthetic consumption, offering an exotic experience of life upon the water. The same space, then, is differently constructed by these two groups of users—a phenomenon that aligns closely with Lefebvre’s thesis of space as social production.

The commodification of Lake Tempe’s space for tourist consumption is also evident in the emergence of floating houses as a tourist destination. Informant 5 noted that “tourists typically arrive in large numbers during August, when they visit the floating houses on Lake Tempe as a destination” (Informant 5, interview, 2025). Floating houses—historically a form of adaptive dwelling developed by Bugis communities in response to fluctuating lake water levels—are now being transformed into objects displayed before tourists as representations of “traditional life upon the water.” This may reflect what tourism scholars describe as the commoditization of culture (Cohen, 1988), in which everyday practices are staged for visitors (MacCannell, 1973). Because we did not interview tourists or floating-house residents, we offer this as a tentative reading rather than a finding.
Of theoretical significance, the pa’tassi phenomenon also reveals a temporal inversion in the spatial logic of Lake Tempe. Informant 5 observed:

“During the rainy season, particularly when flooding occurs, things are somewhat favorable for the pa’tassi, because villagers can only enter and leave the kampong by boat… During the musim timur (East Monsoon), the water recedes slightly, and the waves diminish, so both pa’tassi and fishers find the East Monsoon more profitable” (Informant 5, interview, 2025).

Within the traditional system, the rainy season was the water season—the season for fishing—while the dry season was the land season—the season for cultivation. For the pa’tassi, this logic is inverted: the flood season constitutes their most profitable season, because land-based mobility is impeded, whereas water recession diminishes the very demand for water transport. This inversion is no incidental anomaly; rather, it is the manifestation of an altogether different spatial logic—one in which flooding, which traditional paradigms read as crisis, is reframed within the pa’tassi paradigm as opportunity. This serves as an indicator that post-weir Lake Tempe is not merely losing its older adaptive spaces but is simultaneously cultivating an alternative spatial paradigm rooted in the crisis itself.

Beyond the pa’tassi, another significant new actor in the reconfiguration of Lake Tempe’s space is the NGOs that serve as mediators and advocates. Informant 7, a member of a local policy-oversight NGO, explained the institutional position of his organization:

“This institution accompanies both the community and the government in advocating for Lake Tempe and the weir, and in mediating community concerns. The institution has been engaged in community advocacy for the past two years. The government must take steps to rescue Lake Tempe by undertaking dredging along the lake’s shoreline” (Informant 7, interview, 2025).

NGOs in the Lake Tempe context occupy what, within the Lefebvre (1991) framework, may be designated as actors of representational space—actors who seek to articulate alternative voices against the dominance of representations of space controlled by the state and capital. Informant 7 relayed residents’ view that the ideal water height at the weir is 2 m, a figure he presented as theirs rather than as a technical recommendation. This view sits uneasily with the technocratic rationale for maintaining a high water level (Rifai et al., 2016).

Informant 7’s account suggests that this advocacy has been reactive rather than generative: by his account, his organization became active only two years before our fieldwork, after the effects of prolonged inundation had become acute. We could not establish whether other civil society actors were involved earlier in planning, but his account points to limited institutional space for such participation.

The emergence of these actors has not replaced older ones but has been layered upon them, so that traditional, technocratic, market, and advocacy logics now interact within the same physical space. The post-weir period is therefore better understood as a multidimensional transformation than as a linear story of loss: some spaces persist with declining yields (Palawang, Bungka Toddo, Rawa), others are reported to be no longer practiced (Tanah Koti, Balete), some livelihoods have shifted (farmers into fishing), and new actors have emerged (the pa’tassi and, as advocates, NGOs). This raises the question taken up in the Discussion: how the benefits and burdens of hydraulic intervention are distributed, and for whom post-weir Lake Tempe is being produced.

sec.title: 4. Discussion
sec.p: The findings show that post-weir Lake Tempe is an arena of contested spatial production, in which divergent socio-spatial logics interact, transform, and give rise to new configurations—with direct consequences for the continuity of livelihoods, access to common resources, and the survival of local knowledge around the lake. This section interprets these findings primarily through Lefebvre (1991) theory of the production of space. We draw on the work of Scott (2020) and Wittfogel (1957) on high-modernist and hydraulic states, and on the work of Ostrom (1990) on the commons, only where they help explain specific findings.

The adaptive spatial typology discussed in Section 3.1—Rawa, Palawang, Tanah Koti, Balete, and Bungka Toddo—is most productively analyzed through Lefebvre’s triadic framework of spatial production. Each of these spaces represents what Lefebvre (1991) terms spatial practice (l’espace perçu)—the material dimension in which social practices are enacted routinely and repetitively. The Palawang auction mechanism, the Tanah Koti lottery, and the Balete management application together represent the dimension of representations of space (l’espace conçu)—space as designed and conceptualized by actors invested with formal authority, including the local government, Datu descendants, and capital holders. Meanwhile, the spiritual dimension manifested in the Maccera’ Tappareng ritual, the pamali system of taboos, and the sacred makerre’ sites represents representational space (l’espace vécu)—space as lived through symbol, meaning, and cosmology.

Yet it is precisely here that the present study offers an original contribution to Lefebvrian theory. Lefebvrian theory has been extended to rural spaces (Halfacree, 2007) and to non-Western settings such as revitalized and relocated villages in China (Wang et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2025), but its application to aquatic ecosystems organized by seasonal rhythms remains limited. The Lake Tempe case demonstrates that the dimension of representational space in non-Western agrarian-aquatic societies is not merely artistic or imaginative—as Lefebvre emphasized in his discussions of the spaces of European artists and thinkers—but is also spiritual-religious, structured according to a specific cosmological architecture. The ya makuasae as the entity that rules the waters, the hierarchy of the Macoa Tappareng and the Pabbijagae, and the customary sanction system of idosa with its symbolism of the number eight, together demonstrate that the space lived by the Bugis communities of Lake Tempe is one ontologically interwoven with the supernatural realm.

Lefebvre’s later work offers a way to make this cyclicality explicit. In Rhythmanalysis (Lefebvre, 2013), he treats space and time as inseparable and distinguishes between cyclical rhythms, rooted in natural and cosmic cycles, and linear rhythms, imposed through social and technical routines. Read through this lens, the alternation of water rules and land rules at Lake Tempe is a cyclical rhythm, tied to the flood pulse and marked ritually by Maccera’ Tappareng at the opening and closing of the fishing season. The weir’s target elevation introduces a linear, administratively defined rhythm that overrides this cycle. The pa’tassi’s inverted seasonal logic, in which floods become the profitable season, can in turn be read as a new rhythm emerging from that override.

Analytically, however, the more significant finding is that the dialectic among Lefebvre’s three spatial dimensions at Lake Tempe is not egalitarian but hierarchical. Lefebvre (1991) himself acknowledged the potential for one dimension to dominate the others. At Lake Tempe, the documentary record establishes that the lake’s water level is now regulated by engineering agencies according to a fixed target (Rifai et al., 2016); informants reported that this regime, together with auctions and land titling, has constrained their seasonal practices; and, read through Lefebvre’s triad, we interpret this as a dominance of representations of space over the spatial practice of fishers and farmers and the representational space of customary society. In Lefebvrian terms, the weir’s single target elevation can be read as a homogenization of space—a tendency toward what Lefebvre called abstract space, which subordinates diverse, experiential spaces to one that can be quantified and controlled.

To visualize this interpretation, Figure 3 presents the configuration of the Lefebvrian triad in post-weir Lake Tempe. The three dimensions are shown not as an equilateral configuration but as an asymmetrical one: representations of space, embodied in the weir’s target elevation, the auction system, and land titling, occupy the dominant position and constrain both the spatial practice of fishers and farmers and the representational space of customary society. The five adaptive spaces described in Section 3.1 appear here only as manifestations of spatial practice (see Table 4).

caption.title: Relations among Lefebvre’s three spatial dimensions at Lake Tempe after 2013

sec.p: Figure 3 carries three analytical implications. First, the dominant position of representations of space reflects our reading that authority over the lake’s management has become concentrated in actors whose decisions rest on technical and administrative rather than experiential knowledge of the lake’s rhythms—a shift documented for the weir’s operation and reported by informants for auctions and land titling. This dominance is not absolute: the dotted arrows indicate limited counter-influence, such as gate openings at residents’ request (Rifai et al., 2016) and NGO advocacy. Second, spatial practice and representational space, shown as subordinate nodes, appear in informants’ accounts to have lost much of their capacity to define space. Third, the dashed line between them indicates that the relationship between productive practice and customary cosmology—previously reinforced through the Maccera’ Tappareng ritual and the pamali system—was reported to have weakened. Taken together, these implications support an interpretation, rather than a measured finding, that relations within the triad at Lake Tempe have become more hierarchical—a shift that, in our view, warrants critical scrutiny.

To elaborate on the characteristics and dynamics of each dimension more systematically, Table 6 presents a comparative analysis encompassing dominant actors, operational mechanisms, empirical manifestations at Lake Tempe, relational character, and the status of each dimension following the 2013 operation of the Movable Weir. The table is deliberately structured with the column “Post-2013 Status” placed last in order to underscore that the configuration of the Lefebvrian triad at Lake Tempe is not a static structure but the product of a historical process in which the 2013 infrastructural intervention was a key turning point.

sec.p: Two further frameworks help explain this dominance, though we use them selectively. The thesis proposed by Wittfogel (1957) linking control over water to control over society has been widely criticized for its determinism, and it concerned large-scale irrigation rather than the regulation of floodplain wetlands; we draw only on its core insight that hydraulic management tends to centralize authority. At Lake Tempe, decisions on the lake’s water level now rest with the weir’s operators, although residents’ requests have at times influenced how the gates are operated (Rifai et al., 2016). The concept of legibility proposed by Scott (2020) sharpens this point: a diverse seasonal regime that underpinned five distinct spaces, each with its own access mechanism, has, in our reading, been rendered administratively legible as a single target elevation of +5.00 m. Comparable dynamics have been documented for large dam projects elsewhere, where state visions of modernization marginalize local users (Menga & Swyngedouw, 2018; Müller-Mahn et al., 2021), although the institutional and political contexts of those projects differ from that of a Movable Weir in South Sulawesi.

The reported disappearance of Tanah Koti and Balete can be partly understood through this lens. Both fit poorly into administrative categories: land whose identity changes seasonally and is allocated by lot, and hybrid plots that serve as both paddy and fish trap. Yet legibility alone does not explain their fate. As early as 2016, holders of Tanah Koti were reported to press for the weir to be opened in the dry season so that their land would emerge, while fishers had an interest in keeping the water high (Fajar, 2016). The weir thus entered a field of competing local interests rather than a harmonious community.

This points to a tension that the analysis should not obscure. The pre-weir system was adaptive and locally grounded, but it was not egalitarian. Access to Palawang had already come to depend on financial capital; Tanah Koti was moving from communal usufruct (ongko) toward private ownership through certificates and inheritance by Datu descendants and former officials; and customary rules distributed roles unevenly—women, for instance, were barred from fishing trips under pamali, even as they held ritual roles as Pabbijagae. The weir did not create these inequalities. In our reading, it intensified them by curtailing the seasonal window on which the least capitalized users—lottery-allocated farmers and hybrid farmer-fishers—depended most, while actors with capital could retain Palawang sites through lean years. Spatial justice at Lake Tempe therefore concerns relations within the community as much as relations between the community and the state.

Comparison with other floodplain systems helps situate these dynamics. In the Tonle Sap, upstream dams on the Mekong have altered the flood pulse on which the lake’s fisheries depend (Dang et al., 2022; Soukhaphon et al., 2021), prompting calls to re-operate dams for ecological sustainability (Pokhrel & Tiwari, 2022), while the 2012 abolition of auctioned fishing lots reorganized access around community fisheries (Chan et al., 2020). At Chilika Lagoon in India, sustained mobilization by traditional fishing communities has driven institutional reform (Nayak, 2017). Lake Tempe differs in two respects: the hydrological change is driven by a weir at the lake’s own outlet rather than by distant upstream dams, and collective mobilization among its users has so far been limited and largely reactive.

The analysis has thus yielded three contributions. First, it has shown that Lefebvre’s triad can be extended to a seasonally pulsing, rural-aquatic setting when representational space is understood to include a religious cosmology with institutional effects, and when the cyclical rhythm of space is made explicit through rhythmanalysis. Second, it has traced how relations among the three dimensions became increasingly hierarchical after the weir began operating, with representations of space tending to subordinate both spatial practice and lived space. Third, it has argued that hydraulic infrastructure acted as a compounding force in the erosion of the commons—intensifying enclosure dynamics already underway—rather than as its sole cause. This adds a political-infrastructural dimension to accounts of wetland commons that have foregrounded overexploitation or climate change (Arias et al., 2014; Mammen, 2025).

These findings carry three practical implications, which we frame in terms of process rather than technical prescription. First, the weir’s operating rules would benefit from a review that considers socio-ecological as well as hydrological and economic parameters, including the continuity of customary institutions, fish reproduction, and local livelihoods. The view relayed by Informant 7—that residents regard a water height of 2 m at the weir as ideal—should enter such a review as a community proposal to be evaluated through hydrological, ecological, livelihood, and participatory assessment, not as a recommended operating level; our data cannot establish what level would be appropriate. Second, customary institutions such as the Macoa Tappareng could be formally recognized as participants in lake governance, in line with principles for common-pool resources proposed by Ostrom (1990), with a defined role in deliberations over water levels and access. Given the internal inequalities discussed above, such recognition should be accompanied by attention to who is represented within these institutions, including small-scale fishers and women. Third, local ecological knowledge systems such as Pananrang merit documentation and integration into adaptive management—not as relics of the past, but as knowledge that can inform decisions about seasonal water regimes.

The Lake Tempe case thus speaks to a broader sustainability challenge. As investment in hydraulic infrastructure expands across Southeast Asia, the questions of who designs, who controls, and who bears the costs of spatial standardization are also questions about whether wetland-dependent livelihoods can continue, whether access to common resources remains equitable, and whether local ecological knowledge survives. Lefebvre’s theory—extended to include cosmology and attentive to rhythm—offers a way to make these questions visible in what might otherwise appear to be a purely technical matter of water levels.

sec.title: 5. Conclusion
sec.p: This study has examined how the space of Lake Tempe has been produced and reconfigured amid long-term sedimentation and, since 2013, the operation of the Movable Weir. Before the weir, the lake was organized through the alternation of water rules and land rules into five adaptive spaces—Rawa, Palawang, Tanah Koti, Balete, and Bungka Toddo—bound together by a Bugis-Islamic cosmology expressed in the Maccera’ Tappareng ritual and the pamali system, though already marked by inequalities of access. According to informants, the curtailment of the dry-season recession has left Tanah Koti and Balete no longer practiced, reduced yields in the remaining spaces, and weakened Pananrang, while new actors such as the pa’tassi have emerged from the conditions of prolonged inundation. These changes unfolded over several years and alongside other drivers, including sedimentation, dredging, and hydrometeorological factors.

The case contributes to understanding socio-ecological spatial production in three ways. It extends Lefebvre’s triad to a seasonally pulsing, rural-aquatic setting by incorporating cosmology into representational space and making the cyclical rhythm of space explicit. It suggests how relations within the triad can become hierarchical when hydraulic infrastructure privileges representations of space. And it identifies such infrastructure as a compounding force that intensifies pre-existing enclosure, rather than as the sole cause of the erosion of the commons.

These conclusions should be read in light of the study’s limitations. Because several actor categories are represented by a single informant, recruitment favored locally recognized figures, and fieldwork was concentrated in August 2025, the findings capture positioned accounts within a single season rather than the full range of views within each group or a complete hydrological cycle. The study also cannot establish the relative weight of the weir and other drivers, which would require hydrological and ecological monitoring. Longer fieldwork across a full hydrological cycle, combined with such monitoring and with the inclusion of less visible users such as women and small-scale fishers, would help test and extend these findings.

For participatory and sustainable wetland governance, the findings suggest that the continuity of livelihoods, equitable access to common resources, and the survival of local ecological knowledge depend not only on hydrological targets but also on who takes part in defining them. Decisions about the weir’s operation could therefore include customary institutions and a wider range of lake users, with community proposals—such as residents’ preferred operating level—evaluated through hydrological and participatory assessment rather than set aside.

notes.title: Informed Consent Statement
notes.p: Oral informed consent was obtained from all informants involved in the study and was recorded at the outset of each interview.

notes.title: Data Availability Statement
notes.p: The data supporting the findings of this study consist of confidential interview recordings, transcripts, and field notes, some of which contain sensitive customary knowledge. To protect informants’ confidentiality, in line with the consent obtained and the ethical approval for this study, these data are not publicly available. Anonymized excerpts may be made available from the corresponding author upon reasonable request, subject to informants’ consent and applicable ethical restrictions.
